title: Alert on the last five minutes
hook: A service emits timestamped error events. An alert must show the number in the last five minutes after each new event.
context: Monitoring pipeline with events arriving in timestamp order
solution_brief: Keep a deque of timestamps inside the rolling interval. Append each new event and pop expired timestamps from the front. Each event is appended and removed at most once: O(1) amortized update, O(W) memory for W live events. An unsorted array scan costs O(N) per update; a heap adds O(log N) work that ordered arrivals do not need.

steps.prompt: Events arrive in timestamp order. Which structure lets you add each new event and drop expired ones cheaply?

options.text: A deque: add at the back, remove from the front
An array list, removing expired events from index 0
A stack: push new events, pop expired ones

steps.explanation: Because events arrive in time order, the oldest is always at the front, and a deque adds at one end and removes at the other in constant time. Removing index 0 from an array list shifts every remaining element. A stack only gives access to the newest event, which is never the one that expires.
steps.bottleneck_note: With ordered input, the next thing to expire is always at the front.

steps.prompt: A new event arrives at time t. Which events should be evicted from the front?
steps.explanation: The window is (t − 300, t], open at the old end, so an event exactly 300 seconds old is outside it and must go. A strict less-than keeps it one event too long. Removing only one event per arrival falls behind after a burst.
steps.bottleneck_note: Decide whether the window's boundary is open or closed before writing the comparison.
steps.context_note: The alert counts errors in the last five minutes, and an event exactly 300 seconds old no longer counts.

steps.prompt: Across a stream of N events, what is the amortised cost per event?
steps.explanation: Each event is added once and removed at most once, so the total work across N events is O(N): constant per event on average, even though one arrival may do a lot. O(N) per event would mean rescanning the whole history every time.
steps.bottleneck_note: One expensive step doesn't raise the average when each item is removed only once.
steps.context_note: After a burst, a single arrival evicts thousands of expired events at once.

steps.prompt: What breaks if you keep appending events in the order they arrive?

options.text: The front is no longer guaranteed to be the oldest event
Nothing, because a deque keeps events sorted by timestamp
The late event must be dropped, since it is out of order

steps.explanation: Evicting from the front only works while the front is the oldest event; a late arrival sits behind newer ones and can outstay its window. A deque keeps insertion order, not timestamp order. The usual fixes are buffering for a bounded lateness or indexing by time, because dropping late events undercounts errors.
steps.bottleneck_note: Say whether the window runs on event time or arrival time.
steps.context_note: A network delay delivers an event stamped 10:00:05 after one stamped 10:00:09.

steps.prompt: Eviction only runs when a new event arrives. What does the alert show during those quiet ten minutes?

options.text: The burst's stale count, until something triggers eviction
Zero, because expired events remove themselves after 300 seconds
Zero, because the deque is cleared whenever the window goes idle

steps.explanation: Nothing expires by itself: entries leave only when code runs the eviction loop. If that loop runs only on arrivals, a quiet period freezes the last count on screen. Running eviction on a timer, or when the count is read, lets the alert fall to zero when it should.
steps.bottleneck_note: If eviction runs only on new events, a quiet period freezes the last count.
steps.context_note: Errors stop completely for ten minutes after a burst.
